Rationale.Paragraph: Why the readout moves server-side at all: the owner framed the problem as scalability of access, not as a missing feature — every consumer of the numbers would otherwise need its own Cloudflare account credential (a platform token) or a trip through the personal dashboard, which is exactly the shape the owner rejected ("a dashboard over API" is the requested replacement). One keyed HTTP route on the already-deployed worker turns N token-holders into N key-holders, where the key unlocks daily aggregate counts and nothing else, and rotates in seconds without a redeploy.

Why one credential still exists, and where it lives: the Analytics Engine binding inside a Worker can only write (writeDataPoint); every read path is the SQL REST API, which demands a bearer token. So the choice is not "token vs no token" but "token on machines vs token inside Cloudflare". A Worker secret (dashboard-side, never in the repository, rotatable without redeploy) is the minimal confinement available; consumers hold only the read key.

Why a header and not a query parameter: keys in URLs leak into logs, browser history and shell history by construction; an X-Read-Key header stays out of all three (the live wrangler tail does render request headers, but only to the account holder — an owner-only channel; the spec's pinned guarantee is the branch's own emission bound below). Why exact-match comparison without constant-time machinery: the key is a random high-entropy string, the protected data is daily aggregates with no per-request secret of value, and a timing oracle on a Workers route adds no practical attack surface — the honest residual risk is handled by rotation, which is a seconds-long dashboard edit (and the plan is expected to adopt crypto.subtle.timingSafeEqual — near-zero cost in the Workers runtime, but a Workers-only API: Node 22 does not expose it, so the plan either uses the portable pre-hash alternative in the shared code or shims it in tests — as belt-and-braces on top, with its length-mismatch throw caught and mapped to the same 401, so no uncaught exception can surface a platform error page or a key-length signal).

Why the check order is route shape, then auth, then secret-presence, then cache, then upstream: every check is cheaper and more stateless than the one after it, and pinning the order settles three otherwise-ambiguous outcomes — malformed requests (wrong method, wrong path, stray query) 404 before any key comparison; denial (401) costs zero subrequests on every path; and an unset or empty upstream secret yields 502 even while a stale cache entry exists, so the fail-closed guarantee does not depend on cache warmth. The 10-second abort exists because a hung upstream would otherwise hold the invocation until a platform timeout; it maps to the same 502 as every other upstream failure. The log channel is bounded the same way: the readout branch emits at most one fixed marker constant — never the upstream URL, an upstream response, or any secret — so wrangler tail and Workers Logs cannot become a leak path.

Why tables.mjs must exist: the aggregation today lives inside query.mjs, which executes its CLI switch at import top-level — importable by nothing (a Workers bundle would run the CLI). Extracting the pure renderer into a side-effect-free module gives the worker, the script and the tests one implementation of byDay/fromBreakdown instead of two drifting copies, and makes the /stats response shape and the --dry/--remote prints provably identical by construction.

Why 60 seconds of per-isolate caching: the data is daily buckets read for human eyes; a minute of staleness is invisible, while the cache keeps any accidental polling or a shared bookmark hammering the route from translating into SQL API traffic (per isolate — a polller reaching several PoPs pays one call per isolate per window, still nothing at this volume). Per-isolate is enough — a cold isolate paying one extra query is fine at this volume, and no consistency promise is made across isolates.

Why 401 and not 404-on-deny: the route's existence is public (the README documents it; counting routes are public too), so hiding the auth boundary buys nothing; an explicit 401 keeps the contract honest — key wrong, not resource absent. Why no CORS headers: the consumers are curl/CLI by design; a future browser page is a separate change with its own CORS decision, and absent CORS means a browser cannot read the response cross-origin today (a no-cors request may still be sent — and is harmlessly 404 or 401), which is the safe default.

Terminology: the README section is "Readout access" (not a translation of the owner's Russian "кабинет") — the artifacts speak English, and "cabinet" would read as a cupboard or a .cab file to a native reader; the owner's quoted phrase stays "a dashboard over API" in translation.

Alternatives.Alternative: Per-machine read tokens (the status quo extended): rejected by the owner — a platform-scoped credential on every reading machine does not scale and is exactly what the 2026-11-02 messages reject.

Durable Object or KV counters instead of Analytics Engine reads: rejected — it builds a second storage for data AE already holds, adds runtime cost and a migration of live counting semantics, all to avoid one dashboard-side secret; the C-UPDATER-STATS write path stays frozen instead.

GraphQL API instead of SQL REST: rejected — the SQL API is what query.mjs --live already speaks, so the server-side read is a byte-identical query, and GraphQL would add a second query dialect for no benefit.

Scheduled Worker exporting JSON to a static host (Pages/GitHub): rejected — introduces a second deployed artifact and a staleness/refresh story to gain nothing over serving the live query behind a cache.

Keep the broad wrangler OAuth for future deploys: rejected — a narrow deploy token covers deploy needs at a fraction of the scope, matching the owner's "only a Workers token" instruction; the broad grant is revoked instead.

DeferredDecisions.Decision: An HTML rendering of /stats (a small page or a rich terminal formatter) — deferred until the owner actually wants to look at something prettier than JSON; it would need its own CORS and caching posture.
Multiple or per-person read keys — deferred until more than the owner ever reads the stats; the single shared key is the whole auth model here.
Longer-retention export beyond Analytics Engine's three months — unchanged from C-UPDATER-STATS, deferred there.

Read-side row capping for the readout (a SQL LIMIT or a rendered top-N of from-versions) — deferred: counting semantics are frozen and honest degradation is documented in the Assumptions; capping becomes its own change if junk from-version inflation ever makes the readout unpleasant to read.

The exact minimal deploy-permission set: the README documents both the prebuilt "Edit Cloudflare Workers" template (accurately scoped) and the minimal custom alternative (Account | Workers Scripts | Edit); which one the first redeploy actually requires (e.g. whether re-asserting the custom-domain route needs zone-side rights) is resolved and recorded at that redeploy.

Scenarios.Scenario: Key rotation after a leak: owner edits the STATS_READ_KEY secret in the dashboard; the old key stops working on the next request (auth is checked per request and never cached); no redeploy, no code change, no other consumer coordination beyond sharing the new key.

Analytics token expired or revoked: authorized requests return 502 {"error":"stats-upstream"} once the R-4 cache window has expired (at most 60 seconds of stale 200s may remain on a warm isolate); counting routes keep counting and redirecting unaffected; the owner pastes a fresh token into the secret and the next request after the cache window recovers.

Upstream SQL API outage or hang: non-2XX, network failure, and a call hung past the 10-second abort all map to the same 502; the failed attempt is not cached, so recovery is immediate on the first request after the outage ends.
Cold isolate after a deploy or eviction: the readout cache is empty; the first authorized request pays one upstream query and repopulates; counting routes are indifferent.
Scanner hits /stats without a key: bodyless 401, zero upstream calls — probing the readout costs Cloudflare nothing beyond the Worker invocation itself.

Owner misconfigures a secret as an empty string: an empty STATS_READ_KEY behaves as unset (401, fail closed); an empty STATS_API_TOKEN or STATS_ACCOUNT_ID behaves as unset (502 regardless of cache state) — no fail-open path exists through an empty credential.

C-1.Name: Correct key happy path
C-1.Situation: GET /stats with X-Read-Key exactly equal to the STATS_READ_KEY secret, secrets STATS_API_TOKEN and STATS_ACCOUNT_ID set, upstream SQL API answering fixture rows.
C-1.Expected: 200, application/json, Cache-Control: no-store, body exactly { byDay, fromBreakdown } in the renderTables shape — computed through the shared tables.mjs, identical to what --dry prints for the same rows.

C-2.Name: Auth denial, fail closed
C-2.Situation: GET /stats with a missing X-Read-Key header, a wrong value, or with STATS_READ_KEY unset or set to an empty string.
C-2.Expected: A bodyless 401, and the upstream SQL API is not called at all — the auth check runs before cache and upstream work, so denial costs zero subrequests.

C-3.Name: Upstream secrets absent, before the cache
C-3.Situation: Authorized request while STATS_API_TOKEN or STATS_ACCOUNT_ID is unset or set to an empty string — including when a successful result is still warm in the R-4 cache.
C-3.Expected: 502 with body exactly {"error":"stats-upstream"} — the secret-presence check runs before the cache is consulted, so the mapping holds regardless of cache state; no distinct error reveals which secret is missing.

C-4.Name: Upstream failure and leak guard
C-4.Situation: Upstream SQL API returns non-2XX (including a 403 for an insufficient read-token permission — the worker maps it to the same 502), or the fetch rejects (network), or hangs past the 10-second abort, or the response body is not parseable as JSON.
C-4.Expected: 502 with body exactly {"error":"stats-upstream"}; the response contains no upstream body text, no token, no account id — and neither does any log statement (the branch logs at most a fixed marker constant); the failed attempt is not cached (next request retries upstream).

C-5.Name: Cache window, same isolate
C-5.Situation: A second authorized GET /stats arrives within 60 seconds of a successful one, on the same isolate.
C-5.Expected: 200 served from the module-scope cache with zero additional upstream fetches; a cold isolate simply re-queries once and repopulates; no cross-isolate consistency is promised.

C-6.Name: Counting routes invariant
C-6.Situation: Any counting-route request — /feed valid and malformed, /pkg valid and malformed, unknown paths, non-GET methods — after this change is deployed.
C-6.Expected: Byte-identical behavior to the post-C-UPDATER-REVIEW-FIXES gateway (the archived C-UPDATER-STATS counting semantics with the sibling's wire-shape repairs): same validation, same derived-only Locations, same 404 classes with zero datapoints, same best-effort waitUntil counting; the readout branch and its cache are invisible to these paths, and /stats writes zero datapoints on every path.

C-7.Name: Secrets-name-only scan over the touched files
C-7.Situation: A source scan of every file this change touches (tools/stats-gateway/, the gateway test file, the amended .grace/graph/features.xml and .grace/verification/features.xml entries, the change bundle itself, and .gitignore), comments stripped, after implementation.
C-7.Expected: Only NAMES — the secrets (STATS_API_TOKEN, STATS_ACCOUNT_ID, STATS_READ_KEY) and the credential-family variables (CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, CF_API_TOKEN, CF_ACCOUNT_ID) — the public gateway URL, and the design's fixed non-secret constants appear; no value of any of the three secret shapes (32-hex account id, 64-hex read key, 40-plus consecutive alphanumerics with no separators — so the bundle's own run ids cannot trip it); test fixtures for the secrets use obviously-fake non-hex placeholders; .gitignore carries the .dev.vars and .wrangler entries and no dangling merge marker; wrangler.toml is byte-unchanged.

C-8.Name: Route shape edges
C-8.Expected: 404 in all four cases: shape checks precede auth, so the query-string 404 holds regardless of the key — the handler rejects a non-empty query string explicitly (the /pkg precedent — pathname equality cannot see the query string), the router's exact pathname match rejects /stats/ and /STATS, and the GET-only gate rejects POST before any auth or upstream work.

C-9.Name: Single renderer, import-safe
C-9.Situation: Importing tables.mjs inside the Workers bundler and importing query.mjs inside a test runner.
C-9.Expected: tables.mjs executes nothing on import (pure functions only); query.mjs executes nothing on import (CLI behind a main guard); the aggregation exists in exactly one place, so /stats output and --dry/--remote prints cannot drift.

C-10.Name: Remote mode and its missing-variable error
C-10.Situation: node tools/stats-gateway/query.mjs --remote with STATS_READ_KEY in the environment and the gateway answering fixture JSON (stubbed in tests); then without the variable.
C-10.Expected: The same two tables print as --dry for equivalent rows; without the variable, or with an empty one, the script fails with an actionable error naming STATS_READ_KEY; a non-2XX gateway answer prints the status and the fixed body only and exits nonzero; --live and --dry are unchanged; the usage line lists all three modes.

C-11.Name: README sufficiency for the owner
C-11.Situation: The owner follows the README's "Readout access" section alone, in Safari, without this conversation's context.
C-11.Expected: All three dashboard-side secrets are created and pasted without ambiguity — the token-creation click-path stated (My Profile -> API Tokens -> Create Token), the custom token with the permission exactly as the dashboard shows it (Account | Account Analytics | Read), the account's 32-character ID from the dashboard account home (secret values are not re-viewable after saving, so the docs point at the dashboard, never at the secret), a stated generation command for the read key — rotation-without-redeploy is stated with the dashboard's apply step, secrets are stated as dashboard-side only, the narrow deploy-token flow works from the README alone (accurately scoped template, minimal custom alternative, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID from the dashboard) with the Deployment section carrying the same single credential story, the reading section makes --remote the documented path with the X-Read-Key header named for curl consumers, the Privacy section's datapoint sentence is reconciled (one per valid counting request — the readout writes none), an end-to-end verification step (query.mjs --remote returning the tables, with the failure mapping: 401 = key mismatch; 404 = the deployed gateway predates the readout route — deploy first; 502 = upstream refused or unreachable, including the insufficient-permission case where the fallback permission applies) closes the setup, the rotation apply step, the 403-fallback permission note, the retained readings with their honest limits, the no-embed --live rewrite and the read -s pattern are all present, the broad-OAuth revocation step is present, and no doc line asks for or displays a secret value.
